chapter: The word jazz and the band's New York success
title: Spellings of jazz on Victor records and the New York tryout
summary: He discusses the varied spellings of jazz on early Victor releases, the New York tryouts before the contract, and how the word turned vulgar.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: When we went to New York and we made a great big hit, the word jazz was accepted as a respectable word, as the people didn't know what it meant. First, the Victor Company put the first record out, J-A-S-S. They had four different ways of spelling jazz. Believe it or not, the first way to spell it, J-A-S, I claim none of it. That's my second name. It was the abbreviation of James. I never knew. And I have never claimed it up to today because it never was meant for me because nobody knew my name was jazz in Chicago. After the Victor Company put the Circular's out, these records had worldwide distribution. And they went all over the country. stuff people here in Times-Picayune wrote an article called Jazz and Jazzism which you would contain at your archives.
They spelled it with a double S.

Double S. Now let me tell you how many spellings they had and you can find them. They had J-A-S J-A-S J-A-S-Z around in the 15th and we arrived in New York and we tried out two weeks. Many people think we started on the 26th or 27th. That's not right. We were there before the 7th because we didn't have no uniforms to work with and we went over to Jimmy Balletta's and Nat Levy to get tuxedos fitted up for us and make us look like gentlemen. Now we're coming out of a dive in Chicago and we're going into first class place, one of the largest places in New York and we tried out the Coconut Grove. We tried out at the Paradise. We tried out at the 400 room. We played in the main dining room. All these places we played before we had a contract. And in the paper around the 15th you will find in the telegram J-A-S-Z. They spelled it. J-A-S-Z. They spelled it.

but that ain't the way we give it to them. We spell it J-A to bless. Well, I'm running ahead on something here. The Victor Company first spell it J-A to bless. Then they change it J-A-Z-Z. Some of the young fellas are going with girls, and they take off the J off the front, rub it off with a knife. And they say, you want to hear some good music? Look at the title of that thing. And it was a vulgar word then. It became a vulgar word. It always was a vulgar word to me because that's what I knew it is to be. And our music had that same effect on the dancers. In other words, a lot of people say that we didn't do nothing. They go around and they tell you, oh, this man did this, this one did that. They tell you when they close the district down, that's when they spread jazz. That's not so. Jazz had spread before Joe Oliver came. And not only that, when Joe Oliver made them records, he had young men with him who copied from the Dixieland band. And if anyone cares, listen, I've studied them records. And they're taking Shields part in total. And they're taking part of my first cornet part on the Leverstable Luce. Johnny Dodd uses that.
